young.html: Charles Dickens was the most popular writer in England in the 1800s. When he was twelve, his father was sent to a prison for people who could not pay their debts, and young Charles had to work in a factory pasting labels on bottles of shoe polish. He never forgot it.

In Little Dorrit, a girl named Amy Dorrit is born inside one of those prisons, the Marshalsea. She is small, quiet and very hardworking, and she takes care of her proud father and her whole family. A kind man named Arthur Clennam, just home from far away, wants to help her.

Dickens also makes fun of a government office that never gets anything done, the Circumlocution Office. (Circumlocution means "talking around and around.") Its whole skill, he jokes, is figuring out how not to do things.

young.html: Invent your own office. Dickens gave his office a silly name. Make up a pretend office that makes simple jobs hard, like the Department of Shoe-Tying, and write three of its rules. Then write one rule that would fix it.

full.html: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) published his novels in monthly or weekly parts, read eagerly across Britain and America. In 1824 his father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea prison in Southwark, and twelve-year-old Charles was sent to work in a blacking factory, a humiliation he kept secret for most of his life. Little Dorrit came out in monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, during years when Britain was angry about government bungling in the Crimean War.

full.text: Thirty years ago, Marseilles lay burning in the sun, one day.
full.author: Dickens

full.html: The novel opens in a jail in Marseilles and moves to London, and nearly everyone in it is imprisoned in some way. William Dorrit has lived in the Marshalsea so long that he is called its "Father." His daughter Amy, born there, works quietly as a seamstress to keep the family going. Arthur Clennam, back from twenty years in China, returns to his mother's gloomy house, where she sits in a wheelchair, shut in by guilt and a hidden secret.

full.text: Whatever was required to be done, the Circumlocution Office was beforehand with all the public departments in the art of perceiving—HOW NOT TO DO IT.
full.author: Dickens

full.html: When Arthur tries to find out something simple about the Dorrits' debt, he is sent from office to office, form to form, by members of the Barnacle family, who cling to government jobs like barnacles to a ship. The inventor Daniel Doyce spends years trying to get anyone to look at his useful invention.

full.name: gb-circumlocution
full.cap: Our game version of the Circumlocution Office.

full.html: The book has two parts. In "Poverty," the Dorrits live in the prison. In "Riches," they suddenly inherit a fortune and tour Italy in grand style; William Dorrit, ashamed of his past, wants everyone to forget it, and Amy is lonelier than ever. Meanwhile all London worships the financier Mr. Merdle, until his empire is revealed as a fraud and collapses, ruining those who trusted him, Arthur among them. Arthur ends up in the Marshalsea himself, and Amy comes back to care for him.

full.text: Went down into a modest life of usefulness and happiness.
full.author: Dickens
full.work: Little Dorrit, Book II, last chapter
full.note: Amy and Arthur, newly married, leave the church and go down into the street.

full.html: Dickens's satire of red tape and of a financial bubble made the book controversial; some officials complained it was unfair. His deeper subject is how people imprison themselves, by pride, money or guilt, and how quiet goodness like Amy's sets them free.
Taking Dickens's comic exaggerations as exact history. The Circumlocution Office is invented; but debtors' prisons were real, and Parliament largely ended imprisonment for debt in England in 1869.

items: Dante and Milton pictured prisons of the soul; Dickens finds them in London streets.
Adam Smith and Marx, on this ladder, analyze money and credit; Dickens shows what a bubble does to people.
Balzac in France and Tolstoy in Russia also wrote of families undone or saved by money and pride.
Tocqueville and Mill worried about government that grows clumsy and self-serving; Dickens mocked it.
What kinds of invisible prisons can people live in?
Why is it so hard for a big organization to do simple things?
Does sudden wealth change people? How?
What makes someone like Little Dorrit strong, even though she is quiet?

questions: Little Dorrit took care of her family when she was very young. What do you do to help your family?
Have you ever had to go to many people to get one simple answer? How did it feel?
Why do you think William Dorrit wanted to forget he had been in prison?
Why do people trust someone like Mr. Merdle, who seems rich and important?
The book ends with "a modest life of usefulness and happiness." What would that look like for you?
